bibliographic.title: Mental-LLM: Leveraging Large Language Models for Mental Health Prediction via Online Text Data
bibliographic.authors: Xuhai Xu, Bingsheng Yao, Yuanzhe Dong, Saadia Gabriel, Hong Yu, James Hendler, Marzyeh Ghassemi, Anind K. Dey, Dakuo Wang
bibliographic.venue: Proc. ACM Interact. Mob. Wearable Ubiquitous Technol.
bibliographic.citation_apa: Xu, X., Yao, B., Dong, Y., Gabriel, S., Yu, H., Hendler, J., Ghassemi, M., Dey, A. K., & Wang, D. (2024). Mental-LLM: Leveraging Large Language Models for Mental Health Prediction via Online Text Data. Proceedings of the ACM on Interactive, Mobile, Wearable and Ubiquitous Technologies, 8(1), Article 32. https://doi.org/10.1145/3643540

methodology.method_family: comparative experimental evaluation with zero-shot prompting, few-shot prompting, and instruction fine-tuning
methodology.study_design: multi-LLM benchmark study on mental health prediction tasks using online text data
methodology.sample_description: online text data for various mental health prediction tasks
methodology.technology_context: Alpaca, Alpaca-LoRA, FLAN-T5, GPT-3.5, and GPT-4 evaluated on mental health prediction and exploratory mental health reasoning tasks

eligibility.exclusion_reason: The study centers on benchmarking LLM predictive performance for mental health tasks from online text; it does not examine conversational AI systems, governance mechanisms, accountability, oversight, auditability, or operational control of conversational LLM deployments.
eligibility.decision_rationale: Although the article uses specific LLMs in a regulated-adjacent health domain and briefly notes ethical risks, bias, and deployability limitations, the provided text frames the work as comprehensive model evaluation and performance comparison rather than conversational governance in regulated environments. Python triage over-weighted generic LLM, ethics, and health terms without confirming governance or conversational-system focus.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: Only front matter and a partial introduction were supplied; full-text confirmation is needed to rule out later sections on conversational deployment governance.

appraisal.notes: Appraisal is based only on abstract-level and introductory fragments. The objective and experimental framing are clear, but sampling, data collection, and full analytic procedures cannot be judged from the supplied text.

cerqual.explanation: The abstract presents a coherent empirical benchmark study, but available text is insufficient to assess full methodological adequacy. Relevance to conversational governance in regulated LLM systems is very low because governance, conversational interaction, and operational oversight are not addressed.

coding.theme: LLM performance enhancement for mental health prediction

synthesis.main_claim: Instruction fine-tuning can substantially improve smaller LLMs for mental health prediction tasks and may outperform much larger prompted models, but zero-shot and few-shot designs remain limited and real-world deployment faces important ethical and bias-related constraints.
synthesis.contribution: Provides a broad empirical comparison of multiple LLMs and fine-tuned variants on mental health prediction tasks and summarizes action guidelines for improving LLM capability in this domain.
synthesis.limitations: The authors emphasize important limitations before deployability in real-world mental health settings, including known racial and gender bias and important ethical risks.
synthesis.use_in_review: Exclude as central or supporting evidence for conversational governance. May serve only as distant contextual background on ethics and deployment limits of health-related LLM applications if broader health-risk framing is needed.

evidence.claim: Instruction fine-tuning improves performance across mental health tasks.
evidence.excerpt: our experiments show that instruction finetuning can significantly boost the performance of LLMs for all tasks simultaneously
